**A Friendly Word to the “Good Person”**

You may be kind, honest, generous, and moral. You may be the sort of neighbor everyone admires. And because of that, you may feel you don’t need God.

But the Christian message begins with a truth that humbles every one of us, especially the “good”: **the problem isn’t just what we do, but what we are by nature.**

---

## The Heart of the Matter: Total Depravity

The Bible teaches that sin has touched every part of us—mind, will, heart, and actions. This is called **Total Depravity**. It doesn’t mean we are as bad as we could be, but it does mean that **nothing about us is untouched by sin**, and nothing we do earns God’s favor.

> “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked; who can know it?”  
> — *Jeremiah 17:9*

> “All our righteous deeds are like filthy rags.”  
> — *Isaiah 64:6*

Your good deeds—while praiseworthy in human terms—cannot cleanse a sinful heart. In God’s perfect light, even our virtues are stained. We are **not neutral**, not merely “imperfect,” but **spiritually dead** without Him.

---

## The Shocking Verdict

The Bible doesn’t flatter us:

- “There is none righteous, no, not one.” *(Romans 3:10)*  
- “You were by nature children of wrath.” *(Ephesians 2:3)*  
- “You must be born again.” *(John 3:7)*

So the truth is this: **you are not a “good person” in God’s sight. You are a vile sinner deserving of judgment.**

This is not an insult; it is God’s diagnosis. And only when we accept the diagnosis can we receive the cure.

---

> “Christ died for our sins… He was buried… He was raised on the third day.” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4)

### 5) The Way of Salvation Is Faith, Not Self‑Effort

The Eightfold Path is a road of discipline. The gospel is a **gift**.

> “By grace you have been saved through faith… not by works.” (Ephesians 2:8–9)

You are not saved by attaining enlightenment, but by trusting in the One who died and rose for you.

---

### SEGMENT 1: “A QUESTION BEHIND THE QUESTIONS”

**HOST:**  
Before we jump into objections, let’s admit something: most objections to Christianity aren’t merely intellectual. They’re personal.  
We’ve been hurt. We’ve been disappointed. We’ve wrestled with suffering or hypocrisy. We’ve felt confused or betrayed. And deep down, we all want to know: *Can God be trusted? And if He is, what does He want from me?*

The Bible says God is holy, just, and loving. It also says that **all of us**—every single one—are sinners. That includes religious people and irreligious people. (Romans 3:23)  
So the starting point isn’t pride; it’s humility. We aren’t judges over God. We are creatures who need grace.

---

### SEGMENT 2: “OBJECTION #1: ‘THE CHURCH IS FULL OF HYPOCRITES’”

**HOST:**  
This is a common objection. And honestly, it’s true—there are hypocrites in the church. But here’s the question: **Does the existence of fake things prove the real thing doesn’t exist?**  
If a counterfeit bill exists, it doesn’t mean money is fake. It means money is valuable.

The Bible never says Christians are perfect. It says they are forgiven, being changed, and still needing grace. Jesus even confronted religious hypocrisy more than anyone (see Matthew 23).  
So the real question is not “Are Christians perfect?” The question is: **Is Jesus true?**  
Don’t reject the perfect Savior because of imperfect followers.

---

### SEGMENT 3: “OBJECTION #2: ‘SCIENCE DISPROVES GOD’”

**HOST:**  
This objection is huge in our modern world. But science can only tell us *how* things work, not *why* they exist.  
It can measure the universe, but it can’t explain why there is a universe instead of nothing.  
Many scientists throughout history have been Christians. They saw science as the study of God’s creation.

But the deepest issue isn’t scientific. It’s spiritual. We don’t just need explanations—we need reconciliation with our Creator.

---

### SEGMENT 4: “OBJECTION #3: ‘A GOOD GOD WOULDN’T ALLOW SUFFERING’”

**HOST:**  
This one is heavy. If you’ve suffered, I’m not here to offer simple answers.  
But Christianity doesn’t avoid suffering. It confronts it.

The Bible says sin entered the world through human rebellion, and suffering followed (Genesis 3).  
But God didn’t remain distant. He entered our suffering.  
Jesus was betrayed, mocked, beaten, and crucified. God Himself knows pain—not from a distance, but from a cross.

The Christian message isn’t “You won’t suffer.” It’s “God has entered your suffering and offers redemption through it.”

---

### SEGMENT 5: “OBJECTION #4: ‘CHRISTIANITY IS TOO EXCLUSIVE’”

**HOST:**  
Yes, Jesus said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.” (John 14:6)  
That’s exclusive. But it’s also *inclusive in invitation*.  
Jesus invites *everyone*—every nation, every background, every sinner—to come and be saved.  
No one is beyond His reach. The exclusivity is in the **Savior**, not in the **scope of His invitation**.

Truth is, all worldviews are exclusive in some way. The question is: **Is Jesus true?**  
If He is, then His exclusivity is not arrogant—it’s mercy. It’s God making a clear, accessible way for sinners to be rescued.

---

### SEGMENT 6: “THE CORE PROBLEM: PRIDE—THE CORE SOLUTION: HUMILITY”

**HOST:**  
Every objection eventually confronts the heart.  
At the core is this: **Will I humble myself before God?**  
The Bible says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)

We tend to want a God who affirms us without changing us.  
But Christianity says something more honest: **We need repentance.**  
We are not just broken; we are guilty. And we cannot fix ourselves.

Yet the Gospel is this:  
**Jesus Christ, the sinless Savior, died in our place and rose again.**  
He took the punishment our sins deserved.  
He offers forgiveness and new life to anyone who turns to Him in faith.

That’s the heart of Christianity. Not a system of moral improvement.  
But a rescue.

---

### SEGMENT 7: “SO WHAT NOW?”

**HOST:**  
Maybe today is the day you stop debating and start seeking.  
Maybe it’s time to say, “God, if You’re real, show me.”  
Or maybe it’s time to repent—to turn away from sin and toward Christ.

If you feel the weight of your guilt, that’s not condemnation—that’s conviction.  
God isn’t calling you to shame, but to **life.**  
Jesus said, “Come to Me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.” (Matthew 11:28)

---

### [CLOSING PRAYER / INVITATION]

**HOST:**  
If you’re ready, you can pray something like this:

> “God, I humble myself before You.  
> I confess that I’m a sinner.  
> I need forgiveness and a Savior.  
> I believe Jesus died for my sins and rose again.  
> I turn from my sin and trust in Him.  
> Make me new.  
> Amen.”

---

### [OUTRO MUSIC FADES IN]

**HOST:**  
If you prayed that, or if you have questions, I’d love to hear from you. Reach out. Don’t walk this alone.  
Remember, the Christian faith begins with humility and ends in hope—because Jesus is the only Savior, and He saves completely.

Thank you for listening to *Hope Beyond Objections.*  
Until next time, keep seeking truth—and the One who is the Truth.

**Damnation (Theological Definition)**  
In biblical theology, *damnation* is the literal, final, and irreversible sentence of God against the unrepentant. It is God’s judicial verdict that confirms a person’s guilt and seals their exclusion from His saving presence forever. It is not a temporary discipline or a metaphor for regret; it is a real judgment carried out by the holy Judge of all the earth (Genesis 18:25; Romans 2:5–8; Revelation 20:11–15).

**Why Damnation Is an Act of Holy Wrath**  
God is perfectly holy and cannot overlook sin (Habakkuk 1:13). His wrath is not a loss of control or an emotional outburst; it is His settled, righteous opposition to evil (Romans 1:18). Damnation is the execution of that holy wrath upon those who reject His mercy and remain hardened in sin. The Bible teaches that there is a day when God’s patience ends and His justice is revealed in full (2 Thessalonians 1:6–9). Therefore, damnation is a holy and righteous act consistent with God’s nature.

**Why Hell Is Necessary for Perfect Justice**  
If God is perfectly just, then every sin must receive a just response. Hell is the necessary, final consequence of rejecting God and persisting in rebellion. It is the place of “eternal fire” prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41), and it is also the destination of those who refuse God’s grace (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:10–11). The existence of hell means that God’s justice is complete: evil is punished, righteousness is upheld, and the moral order of the universe is maintained. Without hell, God’s justice would be compromised, and evil would go unanswered.  

In Scripture, the eternal fire is real, unending, and punitive. Damnation is not a temporary corrective; it is the final sentence of God against unrepentant sinners. The gospel declares that salvation is offered in Christ, but damnation remains the just outcome for those who refuse Him.

---

## Teaching for Parents: Total Depravity and Your Children

### 1) What “Total Depravity” Means  
“Total Depravity” does **not** mean that every person is as evil as they could possibly be. It means that **sin has touched every part of our humanity**—mind, will, emotions, and body—so that we are spiritually unable to love God or submit to Him apart from His grace.

### 2) Children Are Not Spiritually Innocent  
Scripture teaches that **all people are born in sin**, not spiritually neutral. This includes our children:

- **Psalm 51:5** – “Surely I was sinful at birth, sinful from the time my mother conceived me.”  
- **Ephesians 2:3** – “We were by nature **children of wrath**, like the rest of mankind.”  

So even the youngest child is not morally blank or innocent before God. By nature, they are **children of wrath**—in the same fallen condition as all humanity.

### 3) “Good” Behavior Is Still Stained by Sin  
Children can do things that appear good—sharing, obeying, showing kindness—but **even their “good” actions are tainted** by sin and self‑centered motives. The problem is not merely bad behavior; it is a **sinful heart**.

- **Isaiah 64:6** – “All our righteous acts are like filthy rags.”  
- **Romans 3:10–12** – “None is righteous, no, not one… no one seeks for God.”

This means that outward goodness does not equal spiritual righteousness. Without God’s grace, even good behavior falls short of true love for God.

### 4) “Slaves to Sin” from Birth  
The Bible describes people as **“slaves to sin”** apart from Christ:

- **John 8:34** – “Everyone who sins is a slave to sin.”  
- **Romans 6:17** – “You were slaves of sin…”

Children are not exceptions. From birth, they are **bound by a sinful nature**, unable to free themselves or choose God on their own.

### 5) Without Supernatural Intervention, They Face the Same Judgment  
Because sin begins at birth and corrupts the heart, **children—like adults—stand under God’s righteous judgment** apart from Christ.

- **Romans 5:12** – “Sin came into the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all men…”

Only **supernatural intervention**—the saving work of the Holy Spirit through the gospel—can rescue them. This is why parents must pray, teach, and depend on God’s grace, not on the child’s natural goodness.

---

## Encouragement to Parents  
The doctrine of Total Depravity is not meant to cause despair but to deepen our dependence on God. It reminds us that:

- **Salvation is by grace alone.**  
- **Children need the gospel as much as adults do.**  
- **God delights to save even the youngest.**  

Parents are called to nurture their children with truth, discipline, prayer, and the gospel—trusting God to give new hearts and faith.

---

### Summary  
Your children are **not spiritually innocent**. They are **children of wrath**, **slaves to sin**, and **even their best behavior is stained** by a fallen nature. Without God’s saving intervention, they stand under the same judgment as the rest of the world from the moment of birth. ## Joshua 11:20 — “Hardened Their Hearts”

> “For it was the LORD’s doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be **devoted to destruction** and receive **no mercy**, but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.” (Joshua 11:20, ESV)

### 1) The Text’s Purpose: Divine Judgment, Not Ethnic Hatred
The conquest narratives present God as judging entrenched, long‑standing evil (cf. Genesis 15:16). The emphasis is not on ethnicity but on persistent wickedness. The Canaanites were not being judged because of their race, but because of their practices and rebellion against God.

### 2) “Hardened Hearts” in Scripture
“Hardening” is a theme throughout the Bible (e.g., Pharaoh in Exodus). It often refers to God *confirming* a person in the direction they have already chosen. That is, God’s hardening is not arbitrary; it is judicial. He gives people over to their own rebellion (see Romans 1:24–28).

This does not remove human responsibility. The Canaanites were already hostile; God’s hardening ensured the confrontation would proceed to judgment.

### 3) The Justice of God and the Limits of Mercy
A core biblical principle is that God is not obligated to show mercy to anyone. Mercy, by definition, is undeserved. This does not make God unjust; rather, it highlights the moral seriousness of evil. Many Christian theologians have affirmed that God, as sovereign and holy, has the right to withhold mercy in order to judge sin fully.

This is not to say God is cruel, but that God is not bound by human expectations. Scripture consistently upholds both His compassion and His justice.

### 4) “No Mercy” and “Utterly Destroyed”
The language of “devoted to destruction” (Hebrew: *herem*) is covenantal and judicial. It is a form of sacrificial judgment—devoting something to God through destruction. The point is not cruelty, but the removal of entrenched evil and the protection of Israel from corrupting practices (cf. Deut. 20:16–18).

### 5) Why Some Interpret This as “Good”
Some interpreters say it is “good” in a moral sense because it demonstrates:
- **God’s holiness:** Evil is not treated lightly.
- **God’s justice:** Sin has consequences.
- **God’s covenant faithfulness:** Israel’s survival depended on God’s action.
- **God’s sovereign freedom:** God is not compelled to extend mercy.

However, even within that framework, many caution against treating judgment as something to celebrate. Scripture models both fear of God’s judgment and sorrow over human sin.

### 6) The Larger Biblical Tension
The Bible holds together two truths:
- God desires repentance and is “slow to anger” (Ezekiel 18:23; 2 Peter 3:9).
- God judges unrepentant evil with real severity.

Joshua 11:20 emphasizes the second truth. It should be read with awareness of the whole canon, which ultimately moves toward the cross—where God’s justice and mercy meet.

---

Joshua 11:20 teaches that God sometimes confirms people in their chosen rebellion so that judgment may fall. At the same time, the broader biblical story urges humility, repentance, and awe before a God who is both perfectly just and abundantly merciful.

## 1) **Corporate Judgment in the Biblical Worldview**
In Scripture, God often deals not only with individuals but with *communities* (e.g., nations, households, and covenant people). Egypt is portrayed as a corporate agent that had:

- **Enslaved Israel** (Ex. 1–2),
- **Defied God repeatedly** through Pharaoh (Ex. 7–12),
- And even **killed Israelite infants** (Ex. 1:22).

The plagues, including the tenth, are presented as divine judgments on a nation’s entrenched rebellion. So the text frames the event as **corporate judgment**, not random cruelty.

---

## 2) **Biblical Teaching on Human Sin and Judgment**
Most classical Christian theology holds that **no human is morally “innocent” in an absolute sense** because humanity is fallen (cf. Romans 3:23; Psalm 51:5). This doesn’t mean infants are personally guilty of the same sins as Pharaoh, but rather that **all human life exists under the reality of sin and death**.

Thus, in the biblical worldview, **death is not an injustice “from God”** but a sober reality of a fallen world. When God judges, He is not taking something He does not own; He is exercising rightful authority over life.

---

## 3) **God’s Sovereignty Over Life and Death**
The text consistently portrays God as the giver and taker of life (Deut. 32:39; 1 Sam. 2:6). This doesn’t make the death of children “easy” or “light,” but it frames it as **God’s prerogative**, not human violence. The biblical view is:

> “Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?” (Gen. 18:25)

If God is truly **holy, omniscient, and just**, then His judgments—even when troubling to us—are not arbitrary or morally deficient.

---

## 4) **The Tenth Plague Is Also a Theological Reversal**
The plague strikes Egypt at the very place where Egypt once struck Israel: the **firstborn**. It is a reversal of Egypt’s earlier slaughter of Hebrew infants (Ex. 1:22). The narrative highlights **measure-for-measure justice**, not random punishment.

---

## 5) **Judgment and Mercy Were Both Offered**
The Passover was not merely an ethnic exclusion; it was **a way of mercy**. The text implies that anyone who trusted God’s word and put the blood on the doorposts would be spared (Ex. 12). Even Egyptians could join Israel afterward (Ex. 12:38). The judgment falls where God’s provision is rejected.

---

## 6) **This Is Descriptive, Not Prescriptive**
Important for teaching: Scripture **describes God’s unique acts of judgment**, but it never licenses human beings to do the same. Only God, who alone knows hearts and governs life, exercises that authority. Humans are never given the right to imitate that judgment.

A traditional Christian defense would say:

- The tenth plague was **corporate judgment** against a nation hardened in rebellion.
- All humans share in the reality of sin and death; therefore the children were **not morally “innocent” in an absolute sense**.

- The event demonstrates God’s **holiness, justice, and sovereignty**, while also preparing for redemption through the Passover.

“Maybe there’s another opportunity after death.”  
“It doesn’t matter what you believe, as long as you’re sincere.”

These are comforting ideas—but they are not the message of Jesus. And the eternal stakes are too high for us to cling to comforting myths.

## Jesus Is the Only Door

Jesus did not present Himself as one path among many. He declared exclusivity:

> “I am the door. If anyone enters by Me, he will be saved.” (John 10:9)  
> “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.” (John 14:6)

If Jesus is telling the truth, then there is no other entrance into life, no parallel track, no post-mortem loophole. The idea of a “second chance” after death is not biblical hope—it is human wishful thinking.

## The Finality of Judgment

Scripture does not present death as the beginning of a new round of choices. It presents it as the end of opportunity:

> “It is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment.” (Hebrews 9:27)

The Great White Throne Judgment is described as the final courtroom of history. There are no appeals, no extra time, no alternative doors. Every person who stands there without Christ is judged by the record of their deeds—and all fall short.

> “If anyone’s name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire.” (Revelation 20:15)

That is not symbolic of a temporary inconvenience. It is the final and eternal consequence for rejecting the only Savior.

## The Reality of the Lake of Fire

We do not like to speak of hell, yet Jesus did. He spoke more about judgment than any other person in Scripture. Not to frighten for fear’s sake, but to warn in love. The Lake of Fire is the destiny of all who refuse Christ’s Lordship—not only those in obvious rebellion, but also those who trust in any other faith, or in no faith at all.

There is no neutral ground. To reject Jesus is to reject the only rescue.

## The Lie of “Tolerance”

The modern virtue of “tolerance” often sounds like kindness, but it denies the very heart of the gospel. It insists that all beliefs are equally valid, and that no one should speak in terms of absolute truth. Yet that very idea becomes a subtle condemnation—because it lulls people into a false security while eternity approaches.

This lie leads to the judgment of the nations: a world that refuses the exclusive Lordship of Christ will stand before the Judge it dismissed. Tolerance promises peace but delivers surprise and terror.

The message of Jesus is not a threat; it is a rescue. There *is* a door. There *is* forgiveness. There *is* eternal life—because Christ died and rose again for sinners.

But the door is not open forever. Today is the day of salvation.

If you have been leaning on the myth of a second chance, let it go. Trust Christ now. Call on Him while you can. There is no other name by which we must be saved.

**Jesus is the only door. Enter while there is still time.**
